$comment: Adversarial JCS canonicalisation cases, shared by every implementation.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. hub/internal/keys and controller/internal/jcs are two
INDEPENDENT implementations of RFC 8785, and that independence is the point:
the hub signs over its canonical form and the controller verifies over its
own, so an implementation that shared code with its counterpart would make
their agreement vacuous. Go's internal/ rule then forbids any single test
from importing both, so agreement cannot be asserted in code — it has to be
asserted against DATA that both read.
proto/vectors already does that for 93 canonical encodings, but those are
the documents this product actually sends: envelopes of integers and short
strings. Nothing exercised the edges where two hand-written canonicalisers
most plausibly disagree — key ordering by UTF-16 code unit, surrogate pairs,
control characters, the ±2^53 boundary, alternative spellings of a number.
The expected values below are derived from RFC 8785 by hand, NOT captured
from either implementation. Captured output would only prove each side
A disagreement here is not cosmetic. It means the hub signs bytes the
controller does not re-derive: every command fails at a gate, or a document
differing from the one a human approved verifies anyway.

cases.name: keys sorted by UTF-16 code unit, not by locale
cases.why: 'A' is 0x41 and 'a' is 0x61, so uppercase sorts first. A locale-aware sort puts them together.

cases.name: a non-ASCII key sorts by its code unit, after ASCII
cases.why: é is U+00E9, above every ASCII letter. Sorting by bytes of some other encoding would reorder this.

cases.name: nested objects are sorted at every level
cases.why: An implementation that sorts only the top level passes most real envelopes.

cases.name: array order is preserved
cases.why: Arrays are sequences; sorting them would change the document.

cases.name: an escaped surrogate pair becomes literal UTF-8
cases.why: RFC 8785 emits everything but the short escapes and control characters literally. Mishandling the pair yields two replacement characters.

cases.name: control characters keep their \u00XX form
cases.why: The short escapes are only \b \t \n \f \r \" \\; everything else below 0x20 is \u00XX, lower-case hex.

cases.name: the short escapes are used where they exist
cases.why: Emitting \u0009 instead of \t is valid JSON and the wrong canonical form.

cases.name: an alternative spelling of zero canonicalises to 0
cases.why: Found by fuzzing. 0e00 is a legal JSON number; a canonicaliser that echoed the spelling would sign different bytes for the same value.

cases.name: a positive exponent is expanded
cases.why: 1e2 and 100 are the same number and must produce the same bytes.

cases.name: the largest exactly-representable integer survives
cases.why: 2^53 is the documented upper bound of the deviation note. One past it must be refused, not rounded.

cases.name: a negative integer keeps its sign
an empty key is a key

refused.name: a non-integer number is refused, not rounded
refused.why: The documented deviation: full ECMAScript double formatting is not implemented, so a real must be an error rather than a guess. Rounding it would sign a number nobody sent.

refused.name: one past 2^53 is refused
refused.why: Beyond the IEEE-754 safe range the value cannot round-trip, so canonicalising it would silently change it.
